raw_case_text:
A 65-year-old, Middle-Eastern male was admitted with a high fever, chills, and vomiting. The symptoms had begun while he was in Liberia, and he came back to Syria as soon as his fever worsened. The patient had no other clinical symptoms and no medical history of other illnesses or drug consumption.
A blood test was performed, and a blood smear was examined under the light microscope (Table 1). He was diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum, and the test was run twice in two different labs. The patient was treated accordingly with artemisinin, 4 tablets per dose twice a day for three days (each tablet contains 20 mg artemether and 120 mg lumefantrine).
Twenty days after malaria treatment, the patient continued to suffer from fever, shivers, and general fatigue. Clinical presentation included pale skin, mucosa, and right hypochondriac pain without jaundice. A blood test with further lab examinations was performed (Table 2).
Blood smears were run for three consecutive days to detect Plasmodium falciparum organisms, while a computed tomography (CT) scan and abdominal echography were also scheduled.
The smears returned negative, and the CT scan revealed liver abscesses (Figures 1 and 2); thus, further tests were required.
A blood test was performed searching for Echinococcus granulosus antibodies and Entamoeba histolytica antibodies, and the test rendered positive results for Entamoeba histolytica.
The abscess was drained as a therapeutic and diagnostic measure, followed by a course of 500 mg intravenous metronidazole every 8 hours for 14 days (Flagyl), to complete the treatment. After improvement, the patient was discharged and instructed to contact his physician if any of his symptoms relapsed, which did not occur.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old male presenting with high fever, chills, and vomiting following travel to Liberia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 65-year-old male developed high fever, chills, and vomiting while in Liberia, prompting his return to Syria as symptoms intensified. He was evaluated and treated for an acute febrile parasitic infection. Twenty days after completing antimalarial therapy, he experienced persistent recurrent fever, chills, generalized fatigue, and new right hypochondriac pain, prompting repeat evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent travel to Liberia. No other prior medical history of chronic illnesses or drug consumption.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation: positive for high fever, chills, and vomiting. Second presentation: positive for persistent fever, chills, fatigue, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Negative for jaundice, diarrhea, or cough. Medications: completed course of artemether-lumefantrine. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Pallor of skin and mucous membranes. Abdomen: right hypochondriac tenderness without peritoneal signs; anicteric. No peripheral lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial blood tests and peripheral blood smears performed. Follow-up evaluation at 20 days: complete blood count demonstrated persistent anemia and elevated inflammatory markers. Repeat peripheral blood smears performed on three consecutive days for intraerythrocytic organisms were negative. Bedside abdominal ultrasound scheduled.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal computed tomography (CT): revealed hepatic abscesses. Serology: Echinococcus granulosus antibodies negative; Entamoeba histolytica antibodies positive. Diagnostic and therapeutic ultrasound-guided percutaneous liver abscess drainage performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute Plasmodium falciparum malaria successfully treated, followed by secondary Amebic liver abscess due to Entamoeba histolytica.
Diagnostic confirmation: Initial light microscopic blood smears performed in two independent laboratories confirmed Plasmodium falciparum; subsequent blood smears over 3 consecutive days confirmed complete malaria clearance; positive Entamoeba histolytica serology, CT imaging demonstrating liver abscesses, and purulent aspiration on drainage confirmed amebic liver abscess.
Treatment & Outcome: Initial malaria treated with artemether-lumefantrine (4 tablets twice daily for 3 days, each containing 20 mg artemether and 120 mg lumefantrine). Amebic liver abscess managed with percutaneous therapeutic drainage followed by intravenous metronidazole (Flagyl) 500 mg every 8 hours for 14 days, resulting in complete clinical recovery without recurrence.
